payload.topic: tc5 CORRECTION -- the deadlock claim was overstated
payload.detail: Correcting my own tc5 statement before it hardens into a false fact. WHAT STANDS, measured: the gauge file is work-area-scoped, both the commander spine and a crew plan in the same directory resolve to one gauge.json, and with no crew running BOTH reported CONTEXT 19 percent matching my fill_fraction 0.193251. Readings are therefore attributed to whichever agent asks, not to whichever agent they measure. That is the defect and it is real. WHAT DOES NOT STAND: I wrote that every relaunched crew trips on arrival before doing any work, and that the relaunch mechanism can never make progress. That was an INFERENCE stated as a measurement, and reading the writer again contradicts it. The hook fires on TOOL USE and both agents write the same file, so the last writer wins -- a crew overwrites the commander's reading with its own on its first tool call, which happens before it runs current or advance. Direct evidence I already had and did not weigh: the gauge carried 0.151219 during the crew's run, which is the crew's own reading, not mine. So the shared file interleaves rather than pins, and a fresh crew most likely reads itself. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE RUN: pass 2 is dispatched now rather than held. The honest severity of tc5 is a wrong-attribution defect with an interleaving race -- a crew can be tripped by the commander's reading if the commander wrote last, and a genuinely full crew can be masked by a small commander's reading. That is still worth fixing and still inverts the safety property; it is not a hard deadlock. LESSON, the same one that cost three passes on D2 earlier in this run: model the behaviour by reading the code that produces it, not by inventing a plausible consequence and asserting it.

payload.decision: ACCEPTED. The gate is NOT blocked on it.
payload.detail: The pass-3 crew escalated rather than deciding, which was right. VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY, not taken on its word: grep across scripts/ and tests/ shows NON_INSTALLABLE_PACKAGES defined once at scripts/install_constellation.py:137 and referenced ONLY at tests/test_install_constellation.py lines 1552, 1557, 1568 and 1575. The installer never reads it at runtime. The crew's report is exact. RULING AND REASONING: the wiring rule exists to catch shipped-INERT CAPABILITY code -- a symbol that passes review and passes tests while no caller ever reaches it. This is not that. It is a POLICY DECLARATION whose enforcement point is the test suite BY DESIGN, and the correct runtime behaviour for a non-installable package is to do nothing, so no production code path could consult it: a package is kept out of the install by never appearing in any skill's required_scripts, and the four guard tests are what make that non-accidental rather than incidental. This is precisely the repo's own two-bin rule from the glossary -- every enforced invariant is either checked by a command or attested by a named human, and prose alone enforces nothing. A frozenset consumed by four guards is bin one, checked by a command. THE DISCRIMINATING EVIDENCE, which is what the wiring rule actually cares about: the declaration is falsifiable -- emptying it turns 3 of the 4 guards red. A symbol that can be broken and caught is not inert, whatever the call-site count says. So the rule fired on a technicality its own purpose does not reach. THE ALTERNATIVE IS REJECTED FOR THIS GATE, NOT DENIED: having discover_skills or validate_required_scripts consult the frozenset at runtime is a real behaviour change to the installer, not a rename, and g0's own constraints forbid unrelated changes here. If it is wanted it gets its own slice. RECORDED SO IT IS NOT REDISCOVERED: 75 of the 76 symbols this gate adds are wired into production code, 178 external call sites total. This is the single exception and it is deliberate.

Then distill what remains into the playbook: write structured delta ops (add [with bank_reason]/confirm/disconfirm/mention/retire/apply/defer — every add/confirm/disconfirm cites a grounding artifact line; corroborate with engine telemetry like rework counts, BLOCK verdicts, waives where possible) to .agent-work/issue-456/lessons-delta.json with tick=true, and apply deterministically: python C:/Programs/constellation-skills/.claude/worktrees/issue-456/scripts/apply_lessons_delta.py .agent-work/issue-456/lessons-delta.json --file .agent-work/LESSONS.md. When you open a PR on Windows, write the body to a temp file and use gh pr create -F <file> — a bash heredoc and a PowerShell @'...'@ here-string both fail for gh pr create --body (here-strings work for git commit -m, not PR bodies). Release must come after that closing advance, never before it — the lease must cover every journaled action, so the release is the final journal entry; releasing earlier leaves archive's own closeout entries (attest/waive/advance) after the lease release and fails the terminal provenance check.

triage_candidates.statement: ENGINE DEFECT (reach-up contract): a HARD context trip blocks 'advance', but 'advance --why' is the ONLY verb that appends a why-record, and the DIGEST line is the latest why-record. So an agent tripped at HARD is forced to hand off carrying a digest that predates the entire step it just completed -- here the digest still describes the context step while understand's four human rulings are absent from it. Doctrine states 'the digest is the brief' for a cold-starting fresh agent (global-everyone.md, reach-up), so the brief is stale exactly when it matters most. Observed live on this run at understand. Candidate fixes: let attest/attach take --why, or add a why-only verb, or have the trip permit a digest-updating advance-in-place. Workaround used: the substance was committed to git and lives in evidence e-understand-1 plus .agent-work/issue-456/interrogation-record.json.

SPEC GAP for the plan checkpoint: DESIGN_SPEC section 2 (Storage layout) ends with 'Build the named guards FIRST' and names three -- (a) the empty-diff determinism assertion, (b) the mis-pairing guard on auto-supersession, (c) the C++ colon collision fix in the relative-id rule. The ranked build queue carries only (a), inside gate 1. (b) attaches to tombstone/auto-supersession machinery the critic panel DEFERRED (SY6); (c) attaches to C++ adapters explicitly OUT OF SCOPE. Both are most likely correctly dropped with the machinery they guard -- but that is the Commander's inference, not a recorded disposition, and 'build first' is strong language to leave dangling. Confirm with Tommy at plan approval: dropped-with-their-machinery, or added to gate 1.

REPO DEFECT (not this issue's scope, found while establishing a baseline): tests/test_mutation_floor.py reports 10 spurious HARNESS ERROR failures for any developer whose environment sets FORCE_COLOR. failed_nodes() at tests/test_mutation_floor.py:255 parses pytest output with the regex '(?:SUB)?FAILED(?:\([^)]*\))? (tests[/\]test_map_orient\.py::\S+)', which requires a literal space between FAILED and the path. With FORCE_COLOR set, the inner pytest subprocess emits ANSI codes ('\x1b[31mFAILED\x1b[0m tests/...'), the regex matches nothing, and the harness reports 'non-zero exit with no FAILED test node' -- i.e. it misreports a CORRECTLY killed mutant as a broken harness. PROVEN: regex vs colored line -> [], vs plain line -> match; FORCE_COLOR=3 is set in this session. test_0_unmutated_baseline_is_green PASSES, so the module under test is fine. CI is unaffected (no FORCE_COLOR, no TTY), so main is genuinely green. Fix: strip ANSI from proc.stdout before parsing, or pass --color=no / PY_COLORS=0 to the inner run_floor subprocess. Worth a ticket: a falsifiability harness that cannot parse its own evidence fails OPEN in exactly the direction it exists to prevent.

TOOLING DEFECT (recover_crews.py) -- a check that cannot discriminate, in the repo's own crew tooling. classify() computes is_alive = bool(alive(entry.get('pid'))). An EXTERNALLY-dispatched crew (--dispatch external / --backend external) has NO pid by construction: the wrapper records the durable entry and spawns nothing, because the crew is an Agent-tool subagent. So alive(None) is False, and a healthy crew three seconds into its work classifies as status=running + pid dead + result missing + resumable -> STATE_RESUMABLE. OBSERVED THIS RUN: constellation/issue-456/g0/implementer/attempt-1 reported RESUMABLE within ~3 minutes of dispatch while the crew was demonstrably alive and working. THE DEFECT IS THE DOCTRINE'S OWN NAMED FAMILY: the output is IDENTICAL in the healthy world (crew working normally) and the defective world (crew died), so the check cannot discriminate however correctly it runs -- see global-orchestrator.md 'A check that cannot fail'. CONSEQUENCE, and why it is not cosmetic: RESUMABLE is in UNRESOLVED_STATES, and both commander-core.md and the spine imperative say to launch ONLY when recovery reports no unresolved running/resumable/conflicting crew. Once any external crew is registered, that precondition can never be satisfied again for this work-id -- it would gate all 22 dispatches of this run (11 gates x implementer+reviewer). Worse, the naive response is to relaunch, and global-everyone.md explicitly forbids launching a continuation into a possibly-sleeping agent's worktree. NOT A DESIGN INTENT: Decision 6 already knows external crews are 'unrecoverable BY THE WRAPPER' and varies the resume ACTION by backend, but leaves the CLASSIFICATION uniform -- so the backend distinction stops one step short of the liveness read that actually needs it. WORKAROUND USED THIS RUN (recorded so it is not mistaken for compliance): treat RESUMABLE-on-an-external-entry as NON-INFORMATIVE, and adjudicate liveness from the artifact set and the subagent's own status per global-orchestrator.md idle-subagent-adjudication -- never relaunch on the wrapper's word alone. CANDIDATE FIX: for an external-backend entry, classify from the result artifact plus an agent-liveness signal (or an explicit dispatched-at + grace window), rather than from a pid that cannot exist.

ENGINE/HOOK DEFECT, DEMONSTRATED: the context gauge is WORK-AREA-scoped, not AGENT-scoped, so an orchestrator and every crew it dispatches share ONE reading -- and the orchestrator's context silently trips the crews. MECHANISM: gauge_writer_hook.resolve_gauge_path derives the file as Path(spine_path).parent / 'gauge.json'. The commander spine (.agent-work/issue-456/spine.json) and the implementer plan (.agent-work/issue-456/g0-implementer-plan.json) live in the SAME directory, so both resolve to the SAME .agent-work/issue-456/gauge.json. The BINDING KEY is already agent-aware -- #419 fixed exactly this class by keying a dispatched agent as session_id#agent_id -- but the PATH is derived from the spine file's parent dir, so the fix stops one step short of the read it needs to protect. PROOF (not inference): with NO implementer running, gauge.json read fill_fraction 0.193251 and BOTH  calls reported 'CONTEXT 19%' -- the commander spine AND the dead crew's plan. The crew has no context to read; it was reporting the commander's. CONSEQUENCE 1, severe: a crew is HARD-tripped by its orchestrator's context. The g0 implementer tripped at a reported 15.1% and correctly filed a refresh-request, but that reading CANNOT BE ATTRIBUTED to it rather than to the commander -- and a trip is indistinguishable from a real one from inside the crew, which is why that crew reasonably diagnosed its own trip as correct. CONSEQUENCE 2, a deadlock: once the orchestrator's own context is over the hard band, EVERY freshly relaunched crew trips immediately on arrival, before doing any work, forever. The relaunch mechanism that reach-up doctrine depends on cannot make progress, because the fresh agent inherits a reading that has nothing to do with it. CONSEQUENCE 3: it also inverts the safety property -- a crew with plenty of headroom is stopped, while a crew genuinely near its limit is invisible whenever the orchestrator happens to be small. CANDIDATE FIX: key the gauge FILE by the same binding key the writer already computes (e.g. gauge-<agent>.json beside the spine, or a per-crew work-area directory), so the reading an engine applies to a plan is the reading of the agent actually driving that plan. Note _is_contained fences the path shape to <root>/.agent-work/<work_id>/gauge.json, so a naive nested-directory workaround is silently dropped rather than separated -- the fence must move with the fix.

GLOSSARY GAP (raised by the g0 implementer, confirmed): the term corpus is overloaded. docs/agents/GLOSSARY.md defines it as 'the full set of installed constellation skills, references, and templates' -- the INSTALLED SKILLS corpus. This issue uses the same word for the set of source files being mapped, and the required symbol name is discover_corpus. Both senses are now live in the same repo and one of them is in a shipped public symbol name, which is exactly what the repo's own one-name-for-one-thing rule forbids. The implementer kept the required symbol name as handed to it and wrote 'mappable corpus' everywhere the distinction mattered, which is the right conservative move but leaves the collision unresolved. RESOLUTION NEEDED: either add a glossary row distinguishing the two senses (e.g. skills corpus vs mappable corpus / source corpus), or rename the derived-map sense before the symbol is load-bearing across gates -- renaming gets more expensive at every later gate, since g1 through gs all build on discover_corpus.

REPO DEFECT, same family as tc3, found by the g0 pass-3 crew and independently reproducible: tests/test_crew_launcher.py::LaunchTests::test_records_entry_before_launch_and_completes does not isolate the environment it asserts about. It asserts PYTHONIOENCODING equals the literal 'utf-8' on the env handed to the launch seam, but scripts/run_crew.py:271 uses env.setdefault('PYTHONIOENCODING', 'utf-8') and its own docstring says that is deliberate -- it honours an explicit caller value without clobbering it. So under any shell that exports a different value the test fails while the PRODUCT BEHAVES EXACTLY AS DESIGNED. The Constellation crew shell exports PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8:surrogateescape, so it fails here for every agent on this machine. Proven in both directions in one sequence: with the ambient value set, 1 failed / 73 passed; with Remove-Item Env:PYTHONIOENCODING, 74 passed. The test is at fault, not the product. FIX: patch.dict(os.environ, ..., clear=...) or pop the var in setUp. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND COSMETICS: this is the SECOND environment-leak false red in this repo's suite after tc3 (FORCE_COLOR defeating the mutation-floor regex), and both share one root -- a test asserting on process environment it does not control. Every crew that runs the full suite at a gate boundary pays a diagnostic detour, and a false red at a gate boundary is exactly the speed bump Tommy's tripwire ruling forbids. WORTH A SWEEP, not just two point fixes: grep the suite for assertions on os.environ-derived values that do not isolate first. NOT FIXED IN THIS RUN, unlike tc3: tc3 blocked all 11 gate boundaries so fixing it was load-bearing; this one fails a single unrelated test that no gate boundary depends on, and the honest gate-boundary number is obtainable by clearing the variable. Fixing it here would be scope creep.

tc8 A gate postcondition PASSED UNEARNED in this very run -- the check could not fail. Item m7 of the g0 implementer job file verified its .gitignore deliverables with a single 'git check-ignore -q' call passed THREE pathnames at once. git treats multiple pathnames with -q as a fatal usage error and exits 128, and the check's leading '!' inverted that non-zero exit into a pass. The check therefore reported PASS in the healthy world AND in the defective world -- it would have passed even if all three files were still ignored. Found and reported by the g0 pass-2 implementer; the engine had already recorded m7 complete on the strength of it. Milder instance of the same family at m9, whose wiring-grep check named only 2 of the 11 symbols the gate added, so it could not see a regression in the other 9. This is precisely the check-that-cannot-fail family issue 456 exists to eliminate, occurring inside 456's own scaffolding, and it is evidence the defect is a live habit rather than a historical one. Fix direction: one check-ignore call per pathname, assert exit 0 per file, and never invert a command whose non-zero exit is ambiguous between 'false' and 'usage error'.

tc9 There is no engine verb for 'the context refresh happened'. Doctrine says a HARD context trip is answered by attaching a refresh-request and handing off at a seam. But once that request is attached, nothing clears it: 'resume' refuses with 'can only resume a blocked gate', and the gate is in-progress, not blocked. The g0 pass-3 implementer hit this and had to work around it. The state machine models the trip and the request but not the recovery, so a refresh-request is write-only -- it accumulates on the item and the only thing that actually unblocks progress is the gauge dropping on its own. Fix direction: either a 'refreshed' verb that closes an open refresh-request, or let 'resume' accept an in-progress gate whose only impediment is an open refresh-request.

tc10 The 'wiring grep' that gate handoffs mandate cannot be a literal grep in this repo, and a literal grep silently fabricates evidence rather than failing. The g0 pass-3 implementer ran the required bare-name search for external call sites of the gate's new symbols and got 4,535 hits, essentially all false: short symbol names collide with unrelated identifiers, prose in markdown, and the symbols' own definitions. It rewrote the check to resolve imports through the AST and got 178 real call sites for 76 symbols. The defect is that the naive form produces a large, confident, entirely wrong number that LOOKS like passing evidence -- a check that cannot fail, in the third route: wrong iteration set. Every remaining gate handoff in this run still mandates the wiring grep in the naive wording. Fix direction: replace the wording in the handoff template with the AST-resolution recipe the implementer already wrote, and treat any wiring count that is implausibly large as a red flag rather than a pass.

tc11 The context gauge lags one tool call behind, so the first engine call after a compaction is refused on a stale pre-compaction reading. Measured directly this run: 'advance g0-implement' was REFUSED with 'context at 27% is at/over the hard limit'; the very next command read gauge.json and found fill_fraction 0.059717 stamped 22:08:53Z; re-running the identical advance then succeeded. The hook writes the gauge AFTER a tool call completes, so the engine reads the value written by the PREVIOUS call. Consequence: the recovery action doctrine prescribes for a HARD trip -- compact, then advance -- fails on its first attempt every time, and reads as a hard deadlock to an agent that does not know to retry. This cost this run one wrongly-declared stop. Compounds with tc5 (gauge is work-area-scoped, not agent-scoped), which makes the stale value potentially another agent's reading as well as an old one. Fix direction: have the engine re-read the gauge after a refusal, or have the refusal message state that the reading is one call stale and a retry is the recovery.

tc12 The 'check' subcommand has zero execution coverage. tests/test_code_map.py:128 asserts only that 'check' PARSES as a subcommand name; nothing calls cli.main(['check', ...]). All 211 lines of scripts/code_map/checks.py could raise on import or at run time with the full suite still green. Found by the g0 reviewer, which ran it by hand (exit 0, full diagnostics) -- but that is a human's hands, not CI. Note the compounding shape: checks.py is the module that PRINTS the page count contradicting render_report.json, so the one artifact that would have exposed the tc-count defect is itself unexercised. Fix direction: g1 rewrites checks.py; give it an execution test at the same time.

tc13 The bundling guard tests are blind below one directory level. ScriptsPackageBundlingTests._source_dirs (tests/test_install_constellation.py:1535-1539) uses a non-recursive iterdir() plus a non-recursive glob('*.py'), so a nested package under scripts/, or a directory whose modules sit one level further down, is invisible to all four guards. The guards do enumerate from the FILESYSTEM rather than from a hand-written list, which is the important half and which they get right -- this is a depth limit, not a hardcoded-list defect. Secondary defect in the same file: test_no_skill_bundles_a_module_from_a_non_installable_package compares BASENAMES, so a future flat scripts/render.py that a skill legitimately bundles would trip it as a false red. Found by the g0 reviewer.

tc14 Dead state and a wrong cross-reference in the shipped code_map package. extract.Extractor.__init__ takes a 'core' parameter and stores self.core (extract.py:256-262); nothing reads it, and the only construction site (extract.py:766) passes the literal True. It is the prototype's slice flag carried into production unexamined. Separately, scripts/code_map/__init__.py:21 points readers at NON_INSTALLABLE_SCRIPT_PACKAGES, but the actual symbol is NON_INSTALLABLE_PACKAGES (scripts/install_constellation.py:135); that comment is the ONLY link between the package and its install-side declaration, so a reader who greps the name the comment gives finds nothing. Found by the g0 reviewer's Fowler speculative-generality pass -- three implementer passes and my own re-verification all walked past the dead field.

tc15 The five rebuildable artifact filenames are duplicated between code and .gitignore with nothing tying them together. They exist as module constants (extract.STATEMENTS_NAME, extract.REPORT_NAME, supplement.SUPPLEMENT_NAME, supplement.REPORT_NAME, render.REPORT_NAME) and again as hand-typed literals at .gitignore:29,30,34,35,36. The narrow one-entry-per-file ignore policy is correct and is not in question; the gap is that renaming a store in code silently starts committing it, with no check that would go red. Found by the g0 reviewer. Fix direction: a test that derives the expected ignore lines from the constants and asserts git check-ignore agrees, one single-pathname call per file per the tc8 lesson.

tc16 An engine rail postcondition is unsatisfiable on a survey controller, so a rail that RAN AND PASSED can only be recorded as a waived risk. The g0 reviewer hit this on r6-fowler, whose SKILL.md instruction is to fill the item's postcondition command with the real record path it wrote. On a survey, no verb can do that: 'amend --op retext-check' is refused with 'amend applies to gated checklists' and 'attest' is refused with 'c1 is engine-checked'. The template also ships c1 with a literal <fowler-pass-record-path> placeholder, which a POSIX shell parses as an input redirection and fails on regardless of the above. The only remaining route was 'waive --force', which frames a passing rail as an accepted risk and makes the record actively misleading about run quality. The reviewer recorded the true reason in the waive text. Fix direction: let retext-check work on surveys, or have 'record' accept the record path as an argument. Same family as tc9 (no verb clears a refresh-request): the state machine models the obligation but not its discharge.

tc17 A real page is silently lost to a case-insensitive filename collision, and it needs a check that can fail. class Verdict (scripts/run_skill_eval.py:178) and def verdict (:407) both resolve to map/scripts.run_skill_eval/Verdict.md, because render.py:405 derives the page filename from key.split(':',1)[1] with no collision check and no case check. This filesystem is case-insensitive and so is CI's windows-latest. I confirmed the surviving file holds the FUNCTION page; the class is unreachable from the map while the module INDEX.md still links to it. Reviewer swept the whole tree and found exactly one collision, no duplicate keys, no module-directory collisions, no invalid filename characters. Second consequence: the map is platform-dependent, so the same source renders 3636 pages on a case-sensitive filesystem, which fails the spec's own determinism falsifier of 'any non-empty diff on unchanged source'. COMMANDER RULING: the collision is NOT fixed at g0 -- renaming is a symbol-identity question and g2 owns symbol identity. Detection is assigned to g1, whose entire charter is a check stage that can fail; g1 must add a page-name collision check that goes red on this exact case, and it cannot write that check if it does not know the case is there. This is populating g1's stated purpose, not expanding its scope. The Fowler pass names the mechanism: primitive obsession -- the supplement key is a bare 'module:Qualified.Name' string that five call sites re-parse by hand, so there is no single place that owns page-name derivation and therefore no single place to put the check.

tc18 'entity_pages' carries the IDENTICAL check-that-cannot-fail defect that B2 fixed, in the same function, and is still wrong. render.py reports entity_pages as len(sizes), and sizes gets one append per emit() CALL, so it reads 3523 while 3522 entity pages exist on disk. It is the same number-that-cannot-go-wrong shape as the 'pages' field: identical output in the healthy world and in a world where pages overwrite each other. The remediation implementer found it, correctly did NOT fix it because the handoff scoped that pass to 'pages' and forbade other defect fixes, and recommended routing it onward. COMMANDER RULING: assigned to g1 alongside tc17, since g1's charter is a check stage that can fail and this is a one-line fix in the function g1 will already be in. Note the lesson for the remaining ten gates: fixing one instance of this defect family does not fix its siblings, so a gate that fixes a cannot-fail check must sweep the enclosing function for the same shape.

tc19 A third environment trap, more dangerous than tc3 and tc7 because it fails SILENTLY GREEN. docs/agents/CREW_CONTEXT.md:19 requires 'python', not 'py'. The py launcher has no pytest installed, so 'py -m pytest' dies with 'No module named pytest' and a careless reader takes it for a clean run. The g0 remediation implementer had already authored 'py -m pytest' into all three of its plan's command postconditions before it found the rule; had it not, the engine would have recorded a verified pass on every gate of that plan on the strength of checks that could not fail -- this issue's own defect class, occurring inside this issue's own scaffolding for the second time (see tc8). It caught and fixed this before starting any gate. Fix direction: add the python-not-py rule to the environment-traps section that every crew handoff now carries, beside FORCE_COLOR and PYTHONIOENCODING; the traps section is demonstrably the field crews actually read.

tc20 The engine has no verb for an author correcting their own not-yet-started plan. The g0 remediation implementer needed to fix three wrong command strings in a plan file it had itself just authored, before 'start' on any gate. 'amend' is the sanctioned route but requires --authority human and no human is reachable from a crew. Its alternatives were to drive four gates through checks it already KNEW were vacuous, or to edit the command text directly. It edited directly, touching no status, satisfied, evidence or journal field, and disclosed the improvisation in its result -- which is the right call and the right disclosure. But the state machine forced a rule-break to avoid shipping a check that cannot fail, which is a bad incentive to leave in place. Fix direction: allow plan-authoring edits to a gate that has never been started, without human authority, since no state or evidence exists yet to protect. Same family as tc9 and tc16: the machine models the obligation but not its legitimate discharge.

tc21 A blunt position grep over the committed page tree will still return 2 hits after B1 is fixed, and a reviewer at gs will read them as B1 unfixed. Both come from a single authored docstring: tests/test_checklist_engine.py's TestGlobToRegex names scripts/checklist_engine.py:449 in its own prose, which the renderer copies through onto the entity page and onto its module index line (tests.test_checklist_engine/TestGlobToRegex.md:8 and INDEX.md:450). This is source text echoed through, not a position the renderer emitted, and it churns only when its own docstring changes -- so by the B1 reasoning it is in the same category as the retained file path and is CORRECT to leave. Recorded so gs is not surprised into re-opening a settled ruling. The remediation implementer also noted it in the test's class docstring. Related: the read-only prototype at .agent-work/issue-456/reference/prototype/render_map.py:159 and render_fn.py:26 still carry the old file:line header, so anyone lifting from the prototype will reintroduce B1.

tc22 A relaunched crew reuses an ABANDONED attempt number, and the resulting registry entry can never be result-verified. Measured this run: two earlier g0 implementer attempts were explicitly abandoned after clean context-trip handoffs; dispatching the remediation implementer registered it as 'constellation/issue-456/g0/implementer/attempt-1' -- the SAME id as the first abandoned attempt -- and reported 'running'. The crew then ran to completion and wrote its result artifact. But 'run_crew.py --verify-result' on that id REFUSED with 'cannot verify an abandoned crew', because the registry still carries the abandoned disposition against the reused slot. So the single mechanism the durable registry exists to provide -- confirming that a dispatched crew actually produced its result artifact -- is unavailable for any relaunched crew, and it fails CLOSED in a way that looks like a policy refusal rather than a defect. I only discovered it because I ran the verification; a commander that trusted the dispatch would never learn the check had not happened. Adjacent to this issue's own defect family: not a check that cannot fail, but a check that cannot RUN, with the same end state of an unverified claim entering the record. Fix direction: allocate a fresh attempt number on every dispatch rather than reusing a terminal slot, and make --verify-result distinguish 'this id was abandoned' from 'this id was abandoned and then relaunched'.

tc23 Sharpens tc22 with a measurement: the two crew-registry tools give CONTRADICTORY dispositions for the same entry. For constellation/issue-456/g0/implementer/attempt-1, run at the same moment: 'recover_crews.py issue-456' reports COMPLETE -- recoverable/complete, do not rerun, while 'run_crew.py --verify-result <same id>' REFUSES with 'cannot verify an abandoned crew'. Both read the same registry. recover_crews is the tool doctrine tells a commander to run before every dispatch to decide whether a slot is clear, and verify-result is the tool that confirms a crew produced its artifact; they disagree, so whichever one a commander happens to consult determines what it believes. A commander following the dispatch precondition alone sees COMPLETE and never learns the result was never verified. Confirmed by re-running verify-result after recover_crews had already reconciled the entry to COMPLETE, so this is not a transient race. Fix direction: one disposition function shared by both tools, and a fresh attempt number on every dispatch so a terminal slot is never reused (tc22).

tc24 CORRECTS tc18, which as I filed it would have misdirected g1 into shipping a second cannot-fail field. tc18 says entity_pages is 'a one-line fix in the same function'. The one-line fix matching g0's own precedent is to count the tree again -- and counting the tree is exactly what the g0 re-review proved is still tautological (B3): pages = sum(1 for _ in out.rglob('*.md')) is a count of the tree it describes, and mutations that delete a quarter of the page tree, remove every module index, or destroy the output layout ALL leave the suite green. So g1 would have 'closed the family' by adding a second field that cannot fail. WHAT g1 SHOULD ACTUALLY DO, ruled: (1) the root is not entity_pages but 'sizes', which feeds three reported fields, so fix the source rather than each field; (2) assert the invariant the report ALREADY contradicts -- pages - 1 - modules against entity_pages, currently 3535 against 3536, differing by exactly the lost Verdict page (tc17); (3) treat a count derived from the same expression as the implementation as no check at all. GENERAL LESSON for the remaining ten gates, and the reason this correction exists: reproducing a falsifier that a crew designed only proves the crew's own probe works. I reproduced both g0 mutation proofs myself and still missed B3, because I never asked whether the test could catch anything OTHER than the probe it was built against. A cannot-fail check must be attacked with a mutation its author did not choose.

tc25 The crew registry became UNDISPATCHABLE for a gate/role, and no documented recovery cleared it. Trying to dispatch the g0 closing implementer: 'run_crew.py --dispatch external' REFUSED with 'refusing duplicate crew: an active attempt already holds g0/implementer@. (status running)', naming attempt-1 -- a crew that had already completed and returned its artifact. Ran the refusal message's own prescribed recovery, 'run_crew.py --abandon <id>': it reported 'abandoned' and the very next dispatch refused identically. Ran it a SECOND time, it again reported 'abandoned', and the dispatch refused identically a third time. Direct inspection of crew-runs.json shows why: slot reuse (tc22) has produced FOUR entries keyed to the same attempt-1 id, of which abandon-by-id resolves one per call while the duplicate check reads a different one, so the two operations can never converge. Meanwhile recover_crews.py reports '0 unresolved' throughout, i.e. the tool doctrine requires before every dispatch says the slot is clear while the dispatcher says it is occupied (tc23). CONSEQUENCE THIS RUN: I could not dispatch the crew, so I made the change myself and disclosed it -- see the ruling on e-g0-review-7. This is now a HARD blocker, not a papercut: a commander that must dispatch an implementer to this gate/role has no working route, and the failure presents as a policy refusal rather than a defect. Fix direction is tc22's -- never reuse a terminal slot -- plus making abandon idempotent over ALL entries sharing an id, and having the duplicate check and recover_crews share one disposition function.

tc26 The render report's page count still cannot notice a zero-byte page -- rglob('*.md') counts a file that was created and never written. Raised by the g0 closing reviewer (its finding A5). tc28 CAUGHT AGAINST THE COMMANDER, and accurate. The engine journal records the advance past g0-review and the attest on g0-integrate precondition p1 roughly eight minutes BEFORE the handoff for the pass that satisfies it existed. The advance itself was legitimate -- g0-review's own postconditions were met -- but attesting 'REVIEW_RESULT received' while both reviews on record read BLOCK makes the journal say the precondition was satisfied by refusals. tc29 A CHECK THAT COULD ONLY EVER FAIL SHIPPED IN THE PLAN, IN ALL 11 GATES. Every gate's c1 postcondition was authored as two shell commands joined by the prose word 'AND'. The engine runs command checks verbatim through a POSIX shell, so the text always died with 'file or directory not found: AND' regardless of the tests. This is the mirror image of the defect shape g0 and g1 exist to hunt: a check that cannot go green is as informationless as one that cannot go red, and nothing between planning and g0-integrate caught it -- gen_execute.py did not validate that a command check parses, and the plan review did not run one. Repaired under amend authority commander (' AND ' -> ' && ', plus env -u FORCE_COLOR -u PYTHONIOENCODING on each half, per tc3/tc7). CANDIDATE: have the engine, or gen_execute.py, refuse to accept a command-kind check whose text does not parse as a shell command -- or at minimum dry-run each command check once at plan time.

tc30 run_crew.py --abandon --relaunch REGISTERS THE NEW ATTEMPT AND THEN HANGS trying to spawn it, leaving a phantom 'running' entry with nothing behind it. Measured at g1: the call timed out at 120s; attempt-2 was already in the registry as 'running', so the next --dispatch external was REFUSED as a duplicate naming a crew that had never started. Same family as tc22/tc25 -- the registry records intent to launch before the launch succeeds, and there is no state for 'registered but never spawned'. Workaround used: --abandon alone (which works), then dispatch the subagent by hand into the already-registered slot. CANDIDATE: make --relaunch register only after a successful spawn, or give the wrapper an explicit 'registered, not started' status that --dispatch can adopt instead of refusing.

tc31 NOTHING IN g1 TIES A PAGE'S LOCATION TO ITS CONTENT. Found by the g1 implementer's undesigned-attack pass: 11 attacks run, 4 survived. Swapping two pages' contents, and renaming a page file, BOTH pass all six g1 checks. The checks verify that the right set of pages exists and that each page is internally consistent, but never that a given page is at the path the map says it is. Deliberately NOT narrowed away in the gate's claims. ROUTE TO g4, whose close criteria already demand a link-following graph walk -- a walk that follows links from INDEX.md would catch both. Do not let g4 close without covering it.

tc32 A GREEN DETERMINISM RUN IS NOT EVIDENCE THAT CALLER ORDERING IS STABLE. Found by the g1 implementer: dropping a sorted() is not uniformly a determinism defect, because a Counter is insertion-ordered and hash-seed-immune, so removing its sort changes nothing observable under a PYTHONHASHSEED sweep. g1's determinism check is real and kills the sorted() drops that DO matter, but its green does not generalise. ROUTE TO g5, which owns caller-split determinism: g5 must establish caller ordering stability by its own argument and must not cite a green g1 determinism run as proof.

tc33 CHECKS THAT DEGRADE QUIETLY RATHER THAN LOUDLY -- four found by the g1 reviewer, none blocking, all real. The sharpest: respelling the inbound line makes refs-line-self-consistent return [] instead of going red, so a rename of the thing it parses silently empties its iteration set rather than failing. That is the 'wrong iteration set' route into a check that cannot fail, and it is the same family as the g0 defects. It is survivable today only because inbound-attribution catches that particular case, which is luck, not design. One assertion fixes it: require the iteration set to be non-empty on a corpus known to be non-empty. ROUTE: fold into gB or wherever the check family is next touched; do not let it sit because a sibling happens to cover it.

tc34: supplement.walk descends node.body ONLY, so any definition inside a compound statement (with/if/try/for) gets NO PAGE AT ALL. Measured by the g2 implementer: one of the four D2 collision members, at tests/test_context_manifest.py:771, sits inside a 'with' block and is invisible to the supplement while extract.py (which uses generic_visit) sees it. The two AST passes DISAGREE about what the corpus contains, and entity_symbol_join cannot see the gap because it iterates supplement keys. This is a real coverage hole in the map AND a blind spot in a g1 check -- any check that iterates supplement keys is blind to these definitions. Route: g4 (schema/top-index) or a dedicated fix; g4 already owns the link-following graph walk.

tc35: the INDEX page-filename collision family is left UNFIXED ON PURPOSE at g2. An entity named INDEX still overwrites its own module's index page. It cannot be fixed at g2 because _make_collision_repo is g1's ONLY cross-platform falsifier for the page-accounting check -- reserving the stem would make that g1 test unable to fail, which is the exact defect this run exists to stamp out. Fixing it requires rebuilding the falsifier on a different collision FIRST, then reserving the stem. Recorded rather than silently swallowed. Note the ordering constraint: falsifier first, fix second.

tc36: TWO defects in the Commander's own g2 handoff, both found by the crew through measurement, both corrected in the attempt-2 handoff. (1) It described the four D2 collisions as 'same-depth siblings' implying four PAGE-level merges; they are four STORE-SYMBOL merges and only three are two-page merges (see tc34). A crew hunting four page pairs would find three and wrongly conclude its own measurement was broken. (2) It prescribed 'env -u FORCE_COLOR -u PYTHONIOENCODING python ...' as the verification form, which the Bash tool REFUSES in a worktree-isolated session ('runs env with -m, whose effect on the command it wraps cannot be verified'). Correct hand-run form is 'unset FORCE_COLOR PYTHONIOENCODING && python ...'; the engine's own POSIX command checks are unaffected. PROCESS LESSON, generalizable beyond this run: a handoff that names an exclusion ('do not weaken any check the previous gate shipped') without naming WHERE the tripwires are makes each successor rediscover them at full cost. The crew named this as the single most expensive thing it rediscovered. Later gate handoffs must carry a per-defect list of the prior gate's tests and mutation anchors that constrain the fix.
